content: 1. Confidentiality in HIV Testing Services (HTS) is paramount. The information shared between the provider and the client must remain private and cannot be disclosed to anyone else without the explicit consent of the individual being tested. However, while maintaining confidentiality, it is essential to avoid perpetuating secrecy, stigma, or shame. Counselors should engage in discussions with clients about whom they may wish to inform about their status and how they would prefer to approach this process. Shared confidentiality, such as involving a trusted partner, family member, or healthcare provider, can often be highly beneficial. 2. Counseling is a critical component of HTS. Pre-test information and post-test counseling can be delivered in group settings when appropriate, but all individuals must have the opportunity to ask questions in a private setting if they wish. Post-test counseling should always be tailored to the specific HIV test result. To ensure high-quality counseling, quality assurance mechanisms, supportive supervision, and mentoring systems should be in place. Various tools and channels, including peer providers and innovative digital approaches like videos, social media, and mobile phone applications, can be utilized to deliver counseling and information effectively. 3. Providers of HTS must prioritize delivering accurate and high-quality testing services. Quality assurance (QA) systems should be implemented to ensure that individuals receive correct diagnoses. QA measures may include both internal and external processes, supported by national reference laboratories. All countries are encouraged to adopt the World Health Organization (WHO) standard three-test strategy for HIV diagnosis. Additionally, individuals who receive a positive HIV diagnosis should undergo retesting to confirm their diagnosis before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) or engaging in HIV care. 4. Effective linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services is essential for individuals diagnosed with HIV. This includes appropriate follow-up and long-term support for prevention and treatment. Providing HTS in areas with limited access to care or poor linkage to services, including ART, offers minimal benefit to those living with HIV. Ensuring linkage to care is the responsibility of HTS providers and testers. Providers may also need to assist individuals in re-establishing or re-engaging with care services if necessary.
